rationale: The candidate reads as one coherent mass across views: a compact block carved into a courtyard/open notch, with the void visible in plan and the stepped/shifted mass legible in oblique views. It responds reasonably to the parcel rather than simply filling it, and the protected courtyard logic gives it a public threshold relation. The access edge is acknowledged, though the ground response is modest and could be sharper. For the neighborhood-living brief, the overall typology is plausible: active ground, one clear void, calm upper mass. The main weakness is sectional clarity: the roof/upper manipulation is somewhat generic and not strongly expressive of a mixed-use section, so the form feels more like a competent cut-and-return mass than a fully articulated sectional building.

reference_assessments.mismatch_warning: More campus-like and terraced than this compact neighborhood brief; avoid over-spreading the mass.
reference_assessments.transferable_principle: Courtyard-and-wing composition with a legible communal void and connected roof/mass hierarchy.

reference_assessments.mismatch_warning: Too single-object and too flat-roofed if copied literally; needs a stronger civic void in this candidate.
reference_assessments.transferable_principle: Simple low-rise pavilion with a clear entry setback and an accommodating street edge.

reference_assessments.mismatch_warning: Counterfactual: the candidate should not become a long sloping section or ramp-dominant figure.
reference_assessments.transferable_principle: Stepped/terraced sectional logic can support neighborhood housing when it preserves a courtyard and ground relationship.

warnings: Visible massing appears to contain some internal compression and stepped subtraction, but the section is not strongly differentiated enough to become a dominant program gesture.
The access-edge response is present but not emphatic; a clearer entry seam or public undercut would better match the brief.
